newsitem.title: UK: Peru author Vargas Llosa stands up for Thatcher.
newsitem.headline: Peru author Vargas Llosa stands up for Thatcher.

text.p: Few serious writers in the world aspire to full-time politics. Still fewer stand up and count themselves admirers of the "Iron Lady", former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

Marios Vargas Llosa, famed as much for his abortive 1990 bid for the Peruvian presidency as his striking novels, is a member of both minority clubs and although the first left him embittered and exiled he has no regrets over the second.
"There are so few writers in the world who admire Margaret Thatcher," Vargas Llosa conceded with a laugh.

"But what she did was extremely courageous. She changed the direction not only of British politics, but world politics," the 61-year-old champion of democracy told an audience at the Edinburgh book festival in a rare public appearance.

Thatcher, who served from 1979 to 1990, was reviled by many British artists and writers who objected to her hectoring style. A Soviet newspaper dubbed her the "Iron Lady" in response to her fierce opposition to communism and socialism.

"She gave to the democratic culture a new impetus. At that time nobody really dared speak in favour of democracy. The democrats were totally convinced that the future of humanity would have a socialist horizon," Vargas Llosa said.
"I think everybody was convinced...but she said: `Why should we have this inferiority complex?'"
Vargas Llosa's own political ambitions foundered, partly on his attempt to convince Peruvians of the merits of Thatcherite economics such as the privatisation of inefficient public services.
The urbane, silver-haired novelist left Peru disillusioned and disgusted after Alberto Fujimori won the election and he now lives in self-imposed exile in London and Spain.

"A writer has an idea of politics which is so remote from the real thing," he said, recalling the idealism which fired his attempts to rescue Peru from economic chaos and the scourge of terrorism in the late 1980s.
"But when you enter the real thing you discover that intrigue and manoeuvring are much more important. It is very destructive for a writer," he said.
Vargas Llosa, who has returned to Peru only twice since losing the election, praised his country's economic stability.

But he has little love for Fujimori and once again voiced accusations that Peru was a "dictatorship" in which human rights abuses were increasing and the media and the judiciary were largely controlled by the government.

Vargas Llosa, whose novels include "Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter" and "Death in the Andes", made clear he had no more political ambitions, saying literature was for him a refuge from the real world.
"I think I have been very lucky. I wanted to be a writer but I never thought I would be the writer I have become...easily published and translated.
"I never dreamed I could make a living from it. For a young Peruvian in the 1950s, to believe he could become a full-time writer was like winning the lottery," he said.
